deep.reconstruction:
PART A (theory of higher congruences, in Kronecker's notation for moduli; (P,p) means modulo p and modulo P(x)).

(A1) Let P(x) in Z[x] have degree nu and be irreducible mod p. Then F = Z[x]/(p,P) is a field with p^nu elements, and x is a generator of F over F_p. Hilbert states:
- x^(p^nu) ≡ x (mod P,p).
- More generally [f(x)]^(p^nu) ≡ f(x) (mod P,p) for every f in Z[x].
- x^(p^mu) is not ≡ x (mod P,p) for mu < nu (meant: 0 < mu < nu).
Reasons (mine, standard): F* has order p^nu - 1, so every element t of F satisfies t^(p^nu) = t. Alternatively, [f(x)]^p ≡ f(x^p) mod p, iterated nu times, gives [f(x)]^(p^nu) ≡ f(x^(p^nu)) ≡ f(x). For 0 < mu < nu, x^(p^mu) = x would put x in the subfield fixed by Frob^mu, of size p^gcd(mu,nu) < p^nu. That contradicts the fact that x generates F.

(A2) Next Hilbert takes polynomials f(X) in a new variable X whose coefficients still contain x, i.e. elements of F[X]. He cites unique factorization into 'Primfunktionen' (irreducibles) modulo (P,p), i.e. in F[X].

Let Pi(X) be prime of degree N. Then the congruence Pi(X) ≡ 0 (mod Pi,P,p) has exactly the N roots X, X^(q), X^(q^2), ..., X^(q^(N-1)), with q = p^nu, and no others. Moreover:
- X^(q^N) ≡ X (mod Pi,P,p).
- X^(q^M) is not ≡ X for 0 < M < N.
This is (A1) repeated one level up, with F_q in place of F_p.

Implicit steps (mine):
- K = F[X]/(Pi) is a field of q^N elements.
- The q-Frobenius fixes the coefficients of Pi (by A1), so each X^(q^i) is again a root.
- These N roots are pairwise distinct because X^(q^M) ≠ X for 0 < M < N.
- A degree-N polynomial over a field has at most N roots, hence 'keine anderen'.
This is the construction of the tower F_p ⊂ F_(p^nu) ⊂ F_(p^(nu N)) and the Galois (Frobenius) description of the conjugates. It is presumably meant as a tool for the question on the previous page: which polynomials split into linear factors modulo prime-power/composite moduli.

PART B (Hurwitz's lemma).
Hurwitz, in his proof of the decomposition into prime ideals, uses the following auxiliary theorem. Write (a_0 x^n + ... + a_n)(b_0 x^m + ... + b_m) = c_0 x^(n+m) + ... + c_(n+m). Then for any coefficients a = a_i and b = b_j, the product ab satisfies an equation
(ab)^N + G_1 (ab)^(N-1) + G_2 (ab)^(N-2) + ... = 0,
where (continued on the next page) the G_k are polynomials in the c's with integer coefficients.

The proof sketch on the next page runs as follows:
- Normalize a_0 = b_0 = c_0 = 1.
- Then a_i and b_j are (up to sign) elementary symmetric functions of complementary subsets of the n+m roots of the c-polynomial.
- The conjugates of a_i b_j under S_(n+m) give a monic polynomial whose coefficients are symmetric, hence integer polynomials in the c's.
- Finally homogenize by c_s -> c_s/(a_0 b_0), a -> a/a_0, b -> b/b_0, and multiply by (a_0 b_0)^N.
The homogenization needs deg G_k ≤ k in c_1..c_(n+m). This is true (my justification): each conjugate has degree ≤ 1 in each root, so G_k has degree ≤ k in each root. A symmetric polynomial of degree ≤ k in each variable is a polynomial of total degree ≤ k in the elementary symmetric functions.
Consequence used for ideal theory: if all c's are algebraic integers, so is every a_i b_j (Dedekind's Prague theorem / Kronecker–Hurwitz content lemma).

Worked case n = m = 1 (mine): (a0 x + a1)(b0 x + b1) = c0 x^2 + c1 x + c2. Then a0 b1 and a1 b0 are roots of Z^2 - c1 Z + c0 c2 = 0, and a1 b1 = c2.
errors: 'x^(p^mu) not≡ x for mu < nu' must exclude mu = 0; correct statement is 0 < mu < nu. The same holds for M < N (0 < M < N).
The dot in f(x^·) and Pi(X^·) is a notational mark, not an operation. The correct congruence is [f(x)]^(p^nu) ≡ f(x) (mod P,p).

In Part B the degree of the equation (written as superscript, N or nu) is unrelated to the degree nu of P in Part A. The next page calls it 'n-ten Grades', which is a slip: the degree is the number of S_(n+m)-conjugates of a_i b_j, not n.

Next-page claim 'G_i homogeneous of degree i in the c' is true only after homogenizing with c_0. In the normalized (c_0 = 1) form G_k is merely of degree ≤ k (and isobaric of weight k(i+j)). The bound is called 'offenbar leicht' without justification but is correct.

results.what: For P irreducible of degree nu mod p: f(x)^(p^nu) ≡ f(x) mod (P,p), and x^(p^mu) ≢ x for 0 < mu < nu
results.modern_name: Frobenius in the finite field F_(p^nu); Galois imaginaries

results.what: Unique factorization of polynomials over F_(p^nu) = Z[x]/(p,P); roots of an irreducible Pi of degree N are X^(q^i), i = 0..N-1, with q = p^nu, and X^(q^N) ≡ X, X^(q^M) ≢ X for 0 < M < N
results.modern_name: Finite field extension F_(q^N)/F_q, Frobenius conjugates, Kronecker modular systems (Pi,P,p)

results.what: If (sum a_i x^(n-i))(sum b_j x^(m-j)) = sum c_k x^(n+m-k), then each a_i b_j is integral over Z[c_0..c_(n+m)] via a monic equation with integer polynomial coefficients in the c's
results.modern_name: Dedekind's Prague theorem / Hurwitz's lemma (content lemma; precursor of Dedekind–Mertens)

deep.surprise_reason: Both parts are standard material of the period. The first is textbook Galois-field theory in Kronecker notation. The second is Hurwitz's lemma, which Hilbert himself explicitly attributes to Hurwitz and later used, with credit, in the Zahlbericht. The page documents Hilbert's reading circa 1894–95, not new results.

X^(p^(M nu)) ≢ X for M = 1 < N = 2
X^(p^nu) is again a root of Pi mod (Pi,P,p)
Hurwitz lemma for n = m = 1: ab = a0*b1 satisfies (ab)^2 - c1*(ab) + c0*c2 = 0, with c1 = a0*b1 + a1*b0 and c0*c2 = a0*b0*a1*b1

transcription_corrections: 'f(x^·)' should be read f(x); the dot is a pen mark or notational marker.
'die π Wurzeln' is probably 'die N Wurzeln' (uncertain).
The exponent in the Hurwitz equation (ab)^nu, (ab)^(nu-1), ... appears in the image as a capital N-like letter, not the nu of Part A.
In the Hurwitz formula the subscript zeros are a_0, b_0, c_0. The closing parenthesis on the right side is unbalanced in the original.
